O adjetivo: conceito e regra da raiz fix: The adjective: the concept and the fixed-root rule
What is an adjective? The grab test. Before any table, a simple question: what is an adjective? An adjective is the word that completes the noun. It is the quality, the characteristic, the way the thing is. And there is an infallible test for recognising it: the grab test. Can you pick up «big» in your hand? No. Can you pick up «new» in your hand? No. Can you pick up «yellow» in your hand? No. But you can pick up a big thing, a new house, a yellow car. You pick up the thing, never the quality. A quality that exists only attached to a noun = adjective. This holds for new, old, tall, short, yellow, red, beautiful, ugly, expensive, cheap, hot, cold, intelligent, strange. They are all adjectives. They all need a noun to exist. And that is why the adjective agrees with the noun. If the noun is masculine, the adjective is masculine. If the noun is feminine, the adjective is feminine. If it is neuter, the adjective is neuter. English adjectives never change, so for you this is new: in Russian, the agreement is very visible, because the ending of the adjective changes clearly and systematically. The golden rule: the root never changes. Here is the information that will set you free. Remember this: every Russian adjective is a LEGO of two pieces: ROOT (untouchable) + ENDING (movable). The root carries the meaning. The ending carries the grammar. So when the adjective has to change gender (masculine → feminine → neuter), the root stays still and only the ending moves. Here is how it looks in Russian with the adjective «new»: The root НОВ- never changed. Only the ending. Always.
A regra de ouro: a raiz nunca muda: The golden rule: the root never changes
A \"tesourinha\": o método para nunca ma: The "scissors" method: how never to get it wrong again

The "scissors" method: how never to get it wrong again. Now the method that will be your tool for the rest of your life. I call it the "scissors": Cut the last two letters of the masculine. You have the root. Paste the new ending. Done — the adjective has changed gender. It works because the masculine endings — -ЫЙ, -ОЙ, -ИЙ — have exactly two letters each. It is a perfect fit. See it in practice: Adjective: но́вый (new) • 1. Cut the last two letters: но́в (root) • 2. Paste the feminine ending: но́в + ая = но́вая • 3. Paste the neuter ending: но́в + ое = но́вое • 4. Paste the plural ending: но́в + ые = но́вые Adjective: большо́й (big) • 1. Cut the last two letters: больш (root) • 2. Paste the feminine ending: больш + а́я = больша́я • 3. Paste the neuter ending: больш + о́е = большо́е • 4. Paste the plural ending: больш + и́е = больши́е Adjective: си́ний (blue) • 1. Cut the last two letters: син (root) • 2. Paste the feminine ending: син + яя = си́няя • 3. Paste the neuter ending: син + ее = си́нее • 4. Paste the plural ending: син + ие = си́ние Did you notice? It is always the same operation. Cut two letters, paste the new one. Always. It never fails. The conclusion that is worth the whole lesson: if you know ONE adjective — the masculine — you know all FOUR. Always memorise the masculine. It is a 75% discount. Want to test it? Take ста́рый (old). Cut the last two letters: ста́р. Now build: ста́р + ая = ста́рая ста́р + ое = ста́рое ста́р + ые = ста́рые You have just learned four forms of an adjective in three seconds. The goal is this: you build the form, instead of merely memorising the ready-made table.
As três terminações do masculino. Antes: The three masculine endings. Before applying the scissors, you need to know which masculine ending the adjective has. There are three possibilities, and each one tells you which "family" the adjective belongs to. • 1. -ЫЙ (the most common) The vast majority of adjectives. Always -ЫЙ in the masculine. но́вый (new) ста́рый (old) краси́вый (beautiful) у́мный (intelligent) холо́дный (cold) дешёвый (cheap) ве́рный (faithful) дли́нный (long) • 2. -ОЙ (when the stress falls on the ending) You recognise it because the stress is at the end. Always -ОЙ in the masculine. большо́й (big) молодо́й (young) дорого́й (expensive) плохо́й (bad) просто́й (simple) родно́й (dear, native) Note: even though it is -ОЙ, you cut the last two letters. The root is БОЛЬШ-, МОЛОД-, ДОРОГ-, ПЛОХ-, ПРОСТ-, РОДН-. • 3. -ИЙ (adjectives with a "special" root) There are two reasons for an adjective to end in -ИЙ: a) Adjectives whose root ends in г, к, х (the throaty consonants). After these consonants, Ы is never written — И is written. It is a Russian spelling rule: ру́сский (Russian) — root РУССК- ма́ленький (small) — root МАЛЕНЬК- ди́кий (wild) — root ДИК- стро́гий (strict) — root СТРОГ- ти́хий (quiet) — root ТИХ- These adjectives behave like ordinary adjectives in the feminine and the neuter: ру́сский → ру́сская → ру́сское ма́ленький → ма́ленькая → ма́ленькое b) The truly "soft" adjectives — the family of синий. A small but important group: си́ний (blue) после́дний (last) у́тренний (morning) вече́рний (evening) весе́нний (spring) зи́мний (winter) ле́тний (summer) осе́нний (autumn) These behave differently: си́ний → си́няя → си́нее (not "си́ная" nor "си́ное"!) после́дний → после́дняя → после́днее It is the only real exception at the start of your studies.
O adjetivo muda com o substantivo: The adjective changes with the noun
O adjetivo vem antes do substantivo e im: The adjective comes before the noun and copies its gender and number. To find the form, start from the masculine (-ый, -ий or -ой) and change the ending: feminine -ая (or -яя), neuter -ое (or -ее), plural -ые (or -ие). After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ you get -ий / -ие (маленький, маленькие, хороший, хорошие). The plural is the same for all three genders. There are four types of adjective, which only change the way the same idea is written: hard (-ый), stressed at the end (-ой), after г/к/х/ж/ч/ш/щ (-ий, and the neuter -ое with stress or -ее without stress) and soft (-ий, -яя, -ее).

A tabela mestra dos adjetivos. Aqui está: The master table of adjectives. Here is the table that solves everything. Notice the beauty of the system: A feminine noun ends in -А/-Я — and the feminine adjective ends in -АЯ/-ЯЯ. A neuter noun ends in -О/-Е — and the neuter adjective ends in -ОЕ/-ЕЕ. A plural noun ends in -Ы/-И — and the plural adjective ends in -ЫЕ/-ИЕ. The system talks to itself. The adjective is a mirror of the noun. A \"família do синий\" — a única exceção: The "синий family" — the only real exception

The "синий family" — the only real exception. In the middle of so many -ЫЙ and -ОЙ lives a small family that ends in -ИЙ and behaves differently. It is the синий family — the only real exception you need to know at the start. The most common members: Notice the difference: The feminine is -ЯЯ (not -АЯ). Си́няя, not "си́ная". The neuter is -ЕЕ (not -ОЕ). Си́нее, not "си́ное". The plural is -ИЕ (not -ЫЕ). Си́ние, not "си́ные". How do you recognise it? If the masculine ends in -ИЙ and the root ends in -н (or a soft consonant), it is probably from the синий family. If the root ends in г, к, х, it is just the spelling forcing -ИЙ (and the feminine is a normal -АЯ). A curiosity: almost all members of the синий family have a time meaning (parts of the day, seasons, "last"). That is a useful pattern for recognising them. And третий? It is the other exception. Тре́тий (third) has the feminine тре́тья (not "тре́тия") and the neuter тре́тье (not "тре́тие"). It is a linguistic fossil, a remnant of an old declension. You just have to memorise it.
A grande confusão: -ИЙ ortográfico vs. -: The big confusion: spelling -ИЙ vs. the -ИЙ of the синий family

The big confusion: spelling -ИЙ vs. the -ИЙ of the синий family. This is a point that is often confusing. Let us take it calmly. There is a Russian spelling rule: after the letters г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ, Ы is never written. И is written. That is why adjectives such as ру́сский (root РУССК-), ма́ленький (root МАЛЕНЬК-), ди́кий (root ДИК-), хоро́ший (root ХОРОШ-), горя́чий (root ГОРЯЧ-) end in -ИЙ in the masculine. But they are not from the синий family. And how do they behave in the feminine and the neuter? Like ordinary adjectives: ру́сский → ру́сская → ру́сское ✅ ма́ленький → ма́ленькая → ма́ленькое ✅ ди́кий → ди́кая → ди́кое ✅ хоро́ший → хоро́шая → хоро́шее ✅ (by the 5-sibilant rule) горя́чий → горя́чая → горя́чее ✅ (by the 5-sibilant rule) That is: it is NOT -яя/-ее. It is -ая/-ое like any ordinary adjective. The ending -ИЙ is only spelling. The rule that separates the two groups: if the root ends in г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ → the -ИЙ is a spelling one → feminine in -АЯ, neuter in -ОЕ, plural in -ИЕ. If the root ends in -н or another soft consonant (the синий family) → the -ИЙ is "real" → feminine in -ЯЯ, neuter in -ЕЕ, plural in -ИЕ. How do you tell which is which in practice? Look at the feminine. If you see "-ая", it is ordinary. If you see "-яя", it is from the синий family. With time you recognise it. A memory trick: the синий family is small. There are about 15-20 adjectives, almost all with a time meaning (seasons, parts of the day) or "last". Everything else that ends in -ИЙ is a normal -АЯ/-ОЕ.
O possessivo concorda com a coisa possuí: The possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner: «моя книга» is said by a man and by a woman alike. In English «my» never changes, so this is new: Russian possessives change with the gender of the thing. The forms «его» (his), «её» (her) and «их» (their) never change. To say who owns something, put the owner's name in the genitive (the form used after «нет»): «сумка Лены» = Lena's bag (English uses 's for the same job).

O acento que passeia (armadilha que ning: Stress on the ending or on the stem (a trap nobody warns you about)

Stress on the ending or on the stem (a trap nobody warns you about). Here is a trap that is almost never explained clearly: Russian adjectives come in two kinds. In some, the stress sits on the ending in every form: -О́Й in the masculine, -А́Я in the feminine, -О́Е in the neuter. In others, the stress stays on the stem. There is no fixed rule. You have to listen and memorise. What to do? Do not try to guess. Copy the form from the table. With time, your ear takes over.
Primeiras frases com «это» e armadilhas: First sentences with «это» and adjective traps
Primeiras frases completas: ЭТО. Uma pal: First complete sentences: ЭТО. One word, one world: э́то (EH-tah — "this is"). It never changes, it agrees with nothing, and it solves the present tense of the verb «to be», which in Russian simply does not appear. Your first dialogue in Russian: — Что э́то? (Shtoh EH-tah? — What is this?) — Э́то кни́га. (EH-tah KNEE-gah. — It is a book.) — Кака́я кни́га? (kah-KAH-yah KNEE-gah? — Which book?) — Но́вая. (NOH-vah-yah. — The new one.) And full sentences, with everything you have learned: The question "which?" also agrees: како́й? (masc.), ка́кая? (fem.), како́е? (neuter), каки́е? (plural). — Како́й дом? — Но́вый. (Which house? — The new one.) — Кака́я кни́га? — Но́вая. (Which book? — The new one.) — Како́е пи́во? — Холо́дное. (Which beer? — The cold one.) Classic traps (announced in advance, so you do not fall into them). ⚠ Mistake 1 — choosing the ending by the thing, not by the noun. English never asks you to do this. "The new house" → ❌ нова́я дом. To a Russian, "нова́я дом" sounds as wrong as "a new houses" sounds to you. ✅ но́вый дом — because дом is masculine in Russian. And "the new book"? Книга is feminine: ✅ но́вая кни́га. The ending of the adjective follows the gender of the Russian noun. ⚠ Mistake 2 — touching the root. ❌ "новова́я". The scissors cut exactly two letters. The root is untouchable. ⚠ Mistake 3 — forgetting that -мя is neuter. ❌ но́вый вре́мя → ✅ но́вое вре́мя (вре́мя is neuter). ⚠ Mistake 4 — mixing up the синий family. ❌ си́ная мо́ре → ✅ си́нее мо́ре (мо́ре is neuter; and the neuter of синий is -ЕЕ). ❌ си́ная кни́га → ✅ си́няя кни́га (синий has the feminine -ЯЯ, not -АЯ). ⚠ Mistake 5 — applying -ЯЯ to adjectives with a root in к, ш, г, х. ❌ ру́сскяя → ✅ ру́сская (the root РУССК- ends in к; -ИЙ is a spelling one, the feminine is -АЯ). ❌ хоро́шяя → ✅ хоро́шая (the root ХОРОШ- ends in ш; -ИЙ is a spelling one, the feminine is -АЯ). ⚠ Mistake 6 — looking for the articles. "A new house" and "the new house" are, in Russian, the same thing: но́вый дом. The articles have disappeared; the context does their job. Breathe a sigh of relief: the eternal doubt "the or a?" is over; it has moved to agreement, and you now know how to do agreement.
